title: Surgical management of ASD, VSD and PDA: anatomy, conduction tissue and repair techniques
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 110 (Congenital Heart Disease)
Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes Cardiac Surgery 4e Ch 19, 20, 22 (ASD, VSD, PDA)
2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease

steps.say: Atrial septal defects are anatomically classified based on their location within the interatrial septum. Ostium secundum defects account for seventy percent of cases and involve the fossa ovalis. Ostium primum defects account for fifteen to twenty percent and represent partial atrioventricular canal defects.
steps.tx: Anatomically, **ostium secundum** defects represent 70 percent of all interatrial communications, arising from deficient fossa ovalis tissue. In contrast, **ostium primum** defects represent 15 to 20 percent and form part of the partial atrioventricular canal spectrum, while **sinus venosus** defects involve caval junctions.

steps.say: Sinus venosus atrial septal defects arise adjacent to the entrance of the superior vena cava. They are strongly associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, where the right upper pulmonary veins drain into the superior vena cava. Surgical repair requires internal pericardial baffling using the Warden procedure.
steps.tx: A superior vena cava type **sinus venosus ASD** is almost universally associated with **partial anomalous venous drainage**, most frequently involving the right superior pulmonary vein into the cava. Surgical correction uses an internal pericardial baffle or the **Warden procedure** to redirect pulmonary venous blood across the defect into the left atrium.

left.title: Warden Procedure Technique
points: Transects superior vena cava above anomalous vein entry
Baffles SVC orifice across sinus venosus ASD into left atrium
Reimplants SVC directly onto right atrial appendage

right.title: Single/Double Patch Baffling
points: Constructs internal pericardial tunnel inside native SVC
Redirects anomalous pulmonary veins through defect
Risk of cavoatrial junction stenosis and sinus node injury

steps.say: Ventricular septal defects are categorized into four distinct anatomical types. Perimembranous defects account for eighty percent of cases and lie directly beneath the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve. Muscular defects are surrounded entirely by myocardium, while supracristal defects lie beneath the semilunar valves.
steps.tx: Ventricular communications comprise four distinct morphologies. A **perimembranous VSD** accounts for 80 percent of defects, situated beneath the septal tricuspid leaflet adjacent to the central fibrous body. Other types include trabecular **muscular VSD** defects, inlet defects, and doubly committed subarterial or **supracristal VSD** lesions.

rows: Perimembranous VSD
Adjacent to membranous septum and tricuspid valve
Conduction bundle runs on posteroinferior margin
Muscular VSD
Entirely enclosed by muscular ventricular septum
Multiple defects (Swiss-cheese septum); spontaneous closure common
Supracristal (subarterial)
Beneath aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves
Aortic cusp prolapse and progressive aortic regurgitation
Inlet (AV canal type)
Beneath tricuspid and mitral valve annuli
Lacks muscular crest between AV valve rings

steps.say: Protecting the specialized conduction system is the highest surgical priority in perimembranous VSD closure. The bundle of His courses along the posteroinferior margin of the defect on the left ventricular side. Sutures must be placed safely on the right ventricular aspect of the crest to avoid complete heart block.
steps.tx: The cardiac specialized **bundle of His** courses along the **perimembranous margin** on the left ventricular side of the septal crest. During surgical patch suturing, placing shallow, bites exclusively on the right ventricular aspect or directly on the tricuspid leaflet base ensures **heart block avoidance**.

nodes.label: Identify perimembranous VSD margins through tricuspid valve
Delineate posteroinferior crest harboring the His bundle
Place pledgeted sutures shallowly on right ventricular surface
Secure Dacron or pericardial patch with zero conduction disruption

steps.say: Supracristal subarterial defects require surgical closure regardless of how small the shunt is. The lack of subpulmonary muscular support leads to prolapse of the right coronary aortic valve cusp into the defect. Progressive cusp distortion produces worsening aortic regurgitation and sinus of Valsalva aneurysm.
steps.tx: A **supracristal VSD** demands prompt surgical patch closure regardless of shunt ratio. The lack of subarterial muscular support exposes the overlying right coronary aortic cusp to high-velocity Venturi suction, precipitating progressive **aortic valve prolapse** and irreversible **progressive aortic regurgitation** if left unrepaired.

left.title: Supracristal VSD Course
points: Lacks muscular infundibular support beneath aortic root
Causes progressive right coronary cusp prolapse
Mandates prompt surgical closure regardless of Qp:Qs

right.title: Small Perimembranous VSD Course
points: Protected by surrounding muscular and fibrous margins
May form tricuspid tissue aneurysm and undergo spontaneous closure
Can be observed safely if asymptomatic with normal hemodynamics

steps.say: Repair of perimembranous and inlet defects is performed through the right atrium. Working through the tricuspid valve under cardiopulmonary bypass avoids cutting ventricular muscle. This transatrial approach preserves right and left ventricular contractility and minimizes late ventricular arrhythmias.
steps.tx: Surgical patch closure of perimembranous and inlet defects is executed via a **transatrial approach** under cardiopulmonary bypass. Working through the retracted **tricuspid valve retraction** zone provides excellent exposure across the defect, achieving reliable **ventriculotomy avoidance** and preserving long-term biventricular systolic contractility and rhythm stability.

nodes.label: Perform median sternotomy and bicaval cannulation on bypass
Open right atrium and gently retract tricuspid valve leaflets
Expose ventricular septal defect without dividing ventricular muscle
Anchor patch with interrupted pledgeted sutures around defect rim

steps.say: Patent ductus arteriosus requires surgical closure when medical therapy fails. In premature infants, persistent shunting causing pulmonary overcirculation and heart failure warrants surgical division. The surgeon exposes the ductus through a left posterolateral thoracotomy without requiring cardiopulmonary bypass.
steps.tx: Indications for **surgical ligation** and division of a patent ductus arteriosus include large left-to-right shunts causing congestive heart failure, pulmonary overcirculation, or failure to wean from ventilatory support, particularly in premature infants with **indomethacin failure** or refractory symptoms despite medical therapy.

rows: Premature neonate
Intravenous indomethacin, ibuprofen, or paracetamol
Medical failure with severe pulmonary edema and renal/gut compromise
Older infant or child
Percutaneous transcatheter coil or plug occlusion
Excessive ductal diameter or unsuitable anatomy for device
Adult with calcified PDA
Endovascular covered stent or surgical division
Symptomatic pulmonary overcirculation or endocarditis

steps.say: Take extreme care to identify the recurrent laryngeal nerve during ductal dissection. The nerve loops directly around the ligamentum arteriosum or ductus before ascending in the tracheoesophageal groove. Dissecting right on the ductal wall prevents nerve traction, hoarseness, and vocal cord paralysis.
steps.tx: During left thoracotomy, the **recurrent laryngeal nerve** must be identified in its critical **ductus relationship**, where the nerve curves directly around the patent ductus arteriosus from anterior to posterior. Meticulous dissection achieves **hoarseness prevention**, protecting against permanent unilateral **vocal cord paralysis**.
